item.title: A System's Approach To Understanding Islam
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
With the rise of Hindu nationalism in India and the subsequent oppression of minorities, it becomes imperative to undertake a critical retrospective on the origins of opposing ideologies, to attempt to debunk the myriad of propaganda with a sliver of truth, and to attempt wherever applicable to foster tolerance and co-existence.

This post is particularly important because 1) any attempt to understand Islam is also an attempt to understand my own identity and 2) all my prior attempts at understanding my own religion ended in failure or confusion or both. I must concede that even this post is not a complete answer that satisfies the original question of identity, rather it is an amateur’s attempt to supply the outlines of an answer where none exists. I must say that this post has given me many nights of anguish and turmoil of heart, nevertheless, we must persevere and ask hard questions, even if no correct answer exists.

Disclaimer: Before we dive in, I must preface that whatever follows is entirely my own personal views and interpretations. There is a tendency for Muslims to get offended before non-Muslims at thoughts like this to which I want to say two things. 1) I do not intend any personal insult, offense, or harm to any other human being, it goes against my religion 2) You may agree or disagree with the ideas presented and I am open to having a rational discussion around it, in fact I would implore such a discussion as God reminds us multiple times in the Qur’an that Islam is for “people who give thought”. My views are pragmatic, derived from experiences of observing the world, people, and phenomena around me like an engineer, a scientist.

There may be contradictions and incompleteness within the text and that’s fine - people still lived before Newton formulated the law of gravity. The goal is to have a workable, practical theory to get away with. This is where I take recluse from the scientific self and appeal to my engineer’s training. If it’s good enough, do not make it better or more crassly put, if it’s working, I do not change it. People may enjoy debating if Plato’s Forms occupy a Divine dimension or the practicality of Nietzsche’s Ubermensch but such debates appear to me as superfluous and hence of little interest. An engineer philosophises only as long as it suits him and no more. Phew, with that out of the way, let us begin.

What is a system?

There are effectively uncountable systems in nature. Out of small moving parts following simple rules, you see extraordinary structure and complexity arising. Cell functions, hurricane formation, economies, ant colonies, a city’s traffic system, biomes - all such arrangement of components that affect change as per their simple local rule and give rise to complex phenomena. Understanding systems is one of the most appealing (see Lorentz attractors). Who wouldn’t want to know what triggers epidemic outbreaks and what contains them? What if you could predict stock market bear and bull markets or business cycles? Unfortunately, it is also one of the most notoriously hard sciences. With the advent of computation, people tried to emulate such systems (Conway’s Game of Life is an introductory system exhibiting such behaviour). I remember taking the distributed systems course in uni and realised how hard it is to design “truly” distributed systems. Some of the most prominent algorithms at the heart of distributed systems (and hence cloud technology and hence underpinning modern existence) are centralised in spirit (see Raft and Paxos algorithms).

How does one even begin to make sense of how these systems behave, characterise them, and then predict its behaviour? There are principles that are essentially heuristics that people have found to hold true. I think these principles are projections of the incomprehensible mechanism that makes the universe tick. What are these principles? Principle of conservation of mass, for example. Or the second law of thermodynamics. These principles have been able to fool our senses for so long that they took the form of “laws”. However, violations have been observed at unconventional scales such as quantum where human senses stop making sense 1 . My guess is that whatever the “theory of everything” is, it can never be understood by humans simply because we are part of the system.

Enough digression, for all practical purposes, the laws are true and they are universal. In particular, it is the concept of entropy that we will continue to revisit. Isn’t it a wonder that life in general appeared in the first place? Look at rocks, they too disintegrate into sand and soil. Everything is broken down and debased. Except the human form. Somehow, lifeless atoms decided to fuse together in special sequences and form amino acids and then nitrates, and phosphates, and then memory carrying DNA. Out of an unimaginable possible history, we find these molecules forming cells and fusing together to form life. What a beautiful day it must have been when the first cell division happened on Earth. No wonder, so many people have tried to recreate “life” (and failed) (See Haldane’s theory and Miller’s experiments) but even though the biologist’s lose hair marvelling at the emergence of life, so does the physicist. Because from a system’s perspective, life locally reverses entropy. It is orderliness created from chaos. It is a contradiction of the most fundamental nature of the universe. Paint never unmixes but somehow cells organise and grow. How can nervous tissue come together to form memory and cognition? The very existence of the human brain contradicts its existence. It is no wonder that all our greatest stories and our greatest religions try to tell where humanity comes from and what its purpose is.

The purpose of religion

Look around you and you will find people who are different – both phenotypically and psychologically. Some are generally joyful, some are bad-tempered, some are greedy, some are kind, and so on. Imagine a civilization of greedy and generous humans, over time greedy folks would end up commanding more resources by hook or crook. Imagine a civilization with mischief driven humans or worst still, of rapist psychopaths who derive hedonistic joy by sacrificing their first born on the altars of their temples. The thing is, as marvellous as the emergence of life itself is, even more marvellous is the illusion of free will. Every man is free to do literally anything which quickly becomes a problem with a little thought. So, humans had to invent boundaries and limits and rules to avoid destabilizing society (The underlying assumption is that it is an implicit goal to survive, of course). I will continue coming back to this point because it’s really important to understand Islam and religion in general. Okay, we need rules so people don’t go around knocking any cute girl up and refuse to take up responsibility for the child, we need rules to make sure the weak also get their sustenance and so on. But why should man follow rules? Man is technically born free. Man follows rules only in two cases 1. If they look up to someone in awe, in admiration or 2. If they fear someone. Most religions present God as a supernatural being to fear and I think it is necessary to reign in man’s passions and wild nature, but it is equally important to appeal to man’s ability to respect things they admire and it is precisely this nature of God that Islam asks you to remember.

The two types of religion

History is replete with examples of men marching into wars and rallying under banners of God to fight crusades and holy wars or whatever. Religion gives men purpose 1 and it is not this functional usage of the word religion that I mean when I use the word “religion” in the following material. For all it matters, I could gather a bunch of people and make them fight others by promising a whole bunch of mangoes if people cared that much about mangoes. Religion is just a convenience here, not a yardstick to measure religion itself.

What’s the other type of religion? The religion of the self, the one that we hold within us, the one that admires God and in that admiration aspires to become closer to God. The religion that nurtures kindness and mercy and appeals to the intelligent mind. The mind that forbids evil and falsehood and enjoins righteousness and honour 2. And believe it or not, it is precisely this that Islam teaches. In fact, those are the exact words I took from the Holy Quran. It is a religion that professes the Jihad of the self - the striving of the self’s mind over the raw passion and unbridled cravings of the body. The word “Jihaad” itself translates loosely into striving or the act of winning over and not whatever is in fashion these days on Indian news channels.

But how does Islamic teachings help stabilize society? Isn’t the last time people tried to centrally plan economies did it fail magnificently? How does Islam reverse entropy? This is because Islam doesn’t only teach to worship God, or how to behave with others, it is a detailed manual for living itself with set rules ranging from personal hygiene to economic systems (Zakaat, for example). Many books have already been written on this topic and a detailed discussion will probably require another book so I will pick three points and try to elucidate.

Surrender to God is closeness to God

The central message of Islam is enshrined in one phrase, “There is no god but God, and Muhammad is His messenger”. It is said that to believe this phrase is to become a Muslim but on careful analysis, one realises it is just an undecidable statement (borrowing a term from mathematical logic) - there is no way a mortal can prove its correctness in the strictest sense of the word. And in fact, the Quran says that even Prophet Muhammad has no idea when the Word and Promise of God (the Judgment Day) will come to pass 2 . Therefore, the choice to believe or not believe lies entirely with the human, it is an exercise of free will. There is no forcefulness, no compulsion in religion 3 . The very act of believing this one statement is to believe in the Quran, in the Hadith, the ways of the Prophet (Sunnah), the Islamic exegesis, the Islamic jurisprudence, and to accept the Islamic way of living. The choice is a voluntary human act of submission and the first step towards complete surrender to God.

As one begins to internalise the teachings of the Prophet, one realises what it really means. There is a well-known Hadith that when a sinful person came to the Prophet asking for guidance, the Prophet only asked him to stop telling lies. And really if you think, lies are the foundation for deceit and instability in society. Lies breeds more lies, sets false expectations, and undermines trust in society. Trust is the bedrock of families and business and hence, of society and economies.

Let’s delve deeper into the lives of great saints and Sufis who are said to have achieved Moksh or salvation. What does it mean to be in a state of eternal happiness? There’s the concept of Ishq-e-haqiqi (Love of the True Divine) which is similar to the state of being completely detached from mortal vestiges of humanly existences such as desire, greed, jealousy and others - a state when the mind truly and only craves the love and approval of the Divine. You may have also read how these small groups of people have to go through long periods of struggle (tapasya) to train their minds into frequenting such states (QUOTE). But what about the rest of us? Is there no way for the great mass of humanity to experience happiness? Yes and I think the answer comes down to that phrase - the first Kalma. It is the degree to which one believes in God that determines their closeness to God. And to be close to God is to yearn to acquire His qualities. What are God’s qualities? Compassionate and Merciful. Have you ever been wronged and struggled for revenge and when the time came, just forgave the offender? There was an attempt to create rife, to create disorderliness and you, as a human exercising free will had a choice and the opportunity, to continue that feud and let countless more suffer but you decided to forgive and show mercy and hence, restore order and stability and peace. That’s how you become closer to God. That’s how one experiences a slice of happiness. And, in my opinion, such happiness is not even accessible to great Sufis and saints.

“The quality of mercy is not strain’d. It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: It blesseth him that gives and him that takes…”

Portia, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4 Scene 1, William Shakespeare

Islam and Wealth

Enough of the abstract, let’s talk about money. There’s a trillionaire in a world where half the population cannot afford basic amenities. How did this happen? If money represents value, are we, as a species, implying that one human is more important than 4 billion other humans? From an economist’s perspective, this is absurd. No human can create such value in society. Therefore, we come to the simple conclusion that money has been decoupled from value. Look closer into the valuations of these companies and you’ll see circular financing, leveraged buy-ins, speculative betting, and a thousand other practices that are designed by humans to inflate the perceived value of these companies. Is this good? Do you know what Islam did 1400 years ago? It anticipated all of it, banned all of it, and made it all sinful in the eyes of the Divine. The health of an economic system is not governed by trickle down logic of capitalism, it is governed by how equitably distributed wealth is within the society. In fact, the concept of obligatory charity is so central to the Muslim that it features along with the five obligatory prayers like a conjoined twin in almost all occurrences in the Holy Qur’an .

On Women

This one is a sensitive topic because any attempts to open a line of dialogue ends up in a chicken fight between men and women - men accusing women of following the sinful ways and women accusing men of being too controlling. Here are my observations: Remember we established that man has a certain nature - some are hedonistic, some are generous, etc. It turns out all men are lustful. That’s their nature, there’s no shame in that. Islam teaches men to acknowledge their nature and to strive against it. It teaches men to discipline their desires. It teaches men to leave behind their vestiges of mortality and to seek the qualities of the Divine. But what about women? What is women’s nature? If men are lustful, what evolutionary pressure birthed the women’s psyche? Think about it, if you were a woman who wanted to breed the next generation of Herculean kids, what would you do? Exhibit! Broadcast and announce your fine breasts and voluptuous body to signal capability to breed healthy kids for your husband and naturally you would seek the best, most athletic, tall, handsome man as your husband. If you think that the urge to dance in Instagram reels or to sell feet pics online are new signs of ignorance (Jahilliyah in Arabic), it’s not. Psychologists and marketers have studied it and used it to sell you all kinds of things (I mean what the fuck is even beauty standards?). And today, it is being amplified to sell false hopes and dreams through social media. It has been proven in multiple studies that social media leads to inferiority complex and all sorts of mental depression and disorders and why not? The human brain is not wired to process so many options, so many competing priorities. How can you expect marriages to be stable when men and women have 100x more options to choose from?

What does Islam say about women? You’ll be surprised to find out and I invite you to do your own research but in spite of all the propaganda that you hear about Islam, it was one of the first religions to grant women rights when the Western world was busy burning women at the stake. Islam codified women’s rights as divine and made it obligatory for men to provide, made it illegal to bear kids without responsibility, and allowed women the right to education and financial independence.

A lot of Islam’s detractors love to point to specific verses from the Quran, ridicule, and try to act all smart. It is nothing but a great show of ignorance and stupidity. One such verse is the verse of the veiled women. But I think nothing is more poetic than the fact that God commands man first (24:30) and then the woman (24:31), for the verse reads:

“˹O Prophet!˺ Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity. That is purer for them. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what they do.”

Surah An-Nur, 24:30, The Holy Qur’an

In my interpretation, the man’s obligation to lower their gaze is more binding on the man than the woman’s responsibility. And why to debate about the greatness of obligation at all if we have already established Islam as striving against the self before anything else – the reward or the punishment is only for the self, then what point is it to blame others or to argue whose obligation is more?

“Whosoever does righteous good deed, it is for [the benefit of] his ownself, and whosoever does evil, it is against his ownself. And your Lord is not at all unjust to (His) slaves.”

Surah Fussilat, 41:46, The Holy Qur’an

Another example is the verse of polygamy revealed at a time when women were treated as objects, abused, and exchanged at will. I sigh and wince when I recall how many of my friends are deluded about polygamy in Islam and the number of times I have had to tell them to go and read instead of just scroll Instagram reels and form their opinions and make it their whole personality. Islam limited the number of marriages to four acknowledging the nature of man and making exploration lawful by marriage whence it comes with responsibilities of a family. In my interpretation, exploration is not free of responsibility, it comes with a cost – a cost made obligatory by Divine law. When I look around, all I find are cheating couples, swapping couples, bored couples, and all kinds of unthinkable Jahilliyah and at the end of it all - misery, chaos, and instability. And I am forced to ask myself, what is better?5 Observe the checks and balances built into the verse itself. It is not a free pass, it is more responsibility.

“If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their ˹due˺ rights ˹if you were to marry them˺, then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four. But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then ˹content yourselves with˺ one or those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession. This way you are less likely to commit injustice.”

Surah An-Nisa, 4:3, The Holy Qur’an

Some folks will come to me and point out “Oh, but look what is the state of women in the Middle East and blah and blah blah”. Sure, but what about women anywhere other than the Middle East? Are they any better? Whenever I scroll news channels all I read are horrendous unthinkable crimes against women and little children. All I can think of is what the fuck is wrong with us? And then I wonder if free access to soft porn, hundreds of young girls dancing in skimpy clothes, and other unthinkable degradations of the human spirit play a role somewhere. Anyways, I often like to point out this analogy to those folks: Imagine an excellent teacher who is teaching a class, the backbenchers do not listen but the studious ones at the front learn and excel in the exam. The backbenchers naturally fail. Would you blame the teacher for the failure of the backbenchers?4

Similarly, Islam doesn’t impose. It invites and invites you to ask questions. If you listen, it’s for your own good.

“Do they not, then, ponder about the Qur’an? Had it been from someone other than Allah, they would have found in it a great deal of discrepancy.”

Surah An-Nisa, 4:82, The Holy Qur’an

Where is humanity going?

Finally, I want to quickly touch up on my thoughts on the second question I asked in the beginning of this discussion. Sure, we may have a somewhat workable pragmatic framework for man’s purpose in life but what about man’s destiny. Here are my thoughts.

We will all become extinct. Our rate of pollution and environmental degradation pushes the Earth’s natural biome beyond the tipping point - the point of no return and our ecosystem spirals into destruction, before we can develop technologies to save it. Seems highly plausible because capitalism never cares about collective good if it doesn’t align with individual enterprise 3. Some people have theorized an ecological reset where an Ice Age or a giant flood (sounds familiar?) wipes out humanity and life restarts again, or the Sun implodes into a red dwarf and engulfs Earth and the other planets, or some capitalist trillionaire figures out a way to send some human embryos to Andromeda. Who knows? The point is, I won’t be there so it doesn’t matter.

Footnotes

1: Although, I hold a slightly more nihilistic view of humanity. I believe there is practically no absolute purpose for mankind. There is no such thing as love. There is only practical convenience and each man is free to choose a purpose.

2: These are words that I am using without definition and it tears my heart. Trust me. Hearing these words it seems like we all kind of “get it” but these are such strong and potent ideas that philosophers have spent centuries trying to define them to no avail. I have not done any better job for myself and still struggle. Our justice system struggles to define such ideas and a lot of the modern struggle strikes directly at the heart of good and evil - whatever those words mean.

3: Don’t get me wrong, I am not a socialist or communist. Capitalism has given us modern wonders such as the internet and vaccines and porn served over high speed internet. Whether they are good for humanity is a different debate, I only outline the nature of capitalism.

4: If you study deeply, you will realise that the rules of Islam are so stringent, that barely anyone is able to follow all of it. Does it mean that no one is a true Muslim? Perhaps, yes. But what it means more is that instead of pointing fingers at others, one should focus on their own behaviours and actions and religion. The religion of the self.

5: I know some smart ass will point out specific cases and say “Oh but I know this and this couple, they are happily married” My friend, Islam is a religion, it doesn’t care about individuals – everyone is differently natured. Islam had to be designed to be widely applicable. Design for the 99%ile is a principle in design theory.

item.title: Meditations from the Beach: Solo Trip To Vizag
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
Couple weeks back, I was working at the exhall which has become like a second home to me, the ambient noise of people who stay away and don’t disturb (mostly), coffee at an arm’s reach, and the hope of occassionally glimpsing my crush1. You get it? Anyways, I was sitting all locked-in, mentally prepared for a deep dive into another one of my rabbit holes when I was disrupted by a senior who loves to chat. I allow him that indulgence since our conversations are stimulating and englightening some times. You should always have a friend to discuss politics with, I think. But this time, we didn’t. Life was getting monotonous so out of curiosity, I just asked him “What can I do as a hobby?” By then, I was joined by a junior and we all sat around that uncomfortable table at CCD.

“have sex”, he said. I sighed. You see, my senior friend is running a little…dry. The kind of friends I have sometimes makes me question myself but then my junior said “Travel”. Not bad, I thought. Not bad for a second (more feasible) option at all. Chatting about tech and the sorry state of India’s investment culture, we ended up at the balcony of Bharti after jumping through a window to get there. I left the building after having booked my flights to Vizag. It would be a week long trip, I will not be taking a leave and I will pretty much plan things as we go along. My flight was on Saturday. I got busy with work for the rest of the week.

Day 1 - Adrenaline high

My flight was at 5 am and I didn’t want to wake up at 3 so I decided to sleep at the airport lounge. I had good portions of protein and fibres from the lounge food and then took to a corner reading some blogpost on my laptop. I had packed Amartya Sen’s Argumentative Indian and Sun Tzu’s classic Art of War with me. I saw people walking in and out, some of them hurried, some of them sleepy, some with whining kids, some with hopes and aspirations. The general song of humanity, you know. I wondered about my own state. How was I feeling? I didn’t know. It seemed like the part which hoped and dreamt was numbed down by the bitter realities as they stood. It would have been great to have a partner on this trip, I wondered. I immediately shrugged off these thoughts - this was it, I am used to it. Everything was going to be fine. Who was I kidding? I could already see nights of writhing and crying. Anyways, we’ll get to it in due time. I have a flight to catch.

I was hoping the trip would give me some clarity and clear out the city fog that seemed to be looming over my mind lately2. Sure enough, I was getting in the headspace, reading Sen, and typing notes ferociously on my notepad. Thoughts were flowing without much effort, there were some spectacular clouds in the air and I was liking it all. A girl was seated in the middle seat and she was tossing her head around in sleep. I found it both a bit cute and distracting. I asked if she wanted coffee or if she would like to rest her head on my shoulder to sleep better. She refused both. Later I found out she was doing her MBA from IIMV. She asked about my reason of visit and I simply said vacation. Workcation to be precise but anyways. She was a typical Delhi girl; I wondered how Indigo managed to mess this up :P

The moisture-laden coastal air hit me but I was on an adrenaline high, booked an Uber and dropped my stuff at the Zostel in Srirampura. The beach was 1.4km away, I set my Fit3 to walking activity and started. It was terribly hot and not the scorching Delhi kind of hot, it was the sweltering, uncomfortable coastal kind of hot. Some of my friends saw my story and rebuked me saying why I went now. I reassured them this wasn’t the worst decision I have taken in my life. I don’t know what I was thinking but I decided to run along the beach road. After pulling an all-nighter, weary from the flight and without any food in my stomach. Yeah. Sue me. I went back to the Zostel, took a bath and planned my day. My junior decided to show up and show me around. I was mentally making notes of things to stock up on - electrolytes, water bottle, power bank. I blinkit-ed all of it that night, got a leaky water bottle, complained to blinkit customer care and they were incompetent little fucks. I also bought a notebook and pencil.

Around 12:30 pm, I had food. Loaded up on carb and protein at a cafe but slightly expensive. I got some fancy hibiscus tea and it was worth it. I synced with my friend here and we went to Rushikonda beach and got drenched trying to click an aesthetic photo. Bought new clothes and it was super cheap (I don’t know living in Delhi conditions people poorly), drank lots of coconut water for 20 rupees a piece (?!). It was around 3pm and God sent clouds so everything was good again. The wind was incredibly delicious. I booked my weekday stay at the Sai Priya resort - slightly expensive but I thought better than a hostel setup especially for work. However, they didn’t have a workspace and I can’t work from bed. We went up to the Thotlakonda monastery by trekking - it was getting dark. Tumbling down the hill and realising of running and racing with another person. I felt like a child for a moment. My fitness band said I burned around 500 kcal so yay I guess.

We explored various random spots. My friend said he knew a spot and then took me to literal heaven. The juxtaposition of the blue of the ocean with the yellow of the sand with the brown of the rugged rocks with the green of the hill and the white of the clouds. It was magnificent.

My friend effortlessly engaged the locals and we got dirt cheap local commute - at one point, literally hanging from the back of a shared auto. Bumping head on the ceiling when passing over a bumper. Had to tilt my head just to see because my eyes were obstructed by the tarpoline of the auto’s top. Rickshaw wale bhaiya had zero chills, he was zooming past palm trees after palm trees as the cool air made things better. Great experience. Locals were so nice and wanted to help you out without taking advantage. Again, my mind wandered to Delhi folks and the a priori conditioning that people are always unruly and loud and disobedient and selfish.

I slept at 9pm that day for like eight hours.

Day 2 - Meditation and Solitude

I packed some basics and went out for a run on the beach road. They had cordoned off traffic for the stretch and there were people - locals, athletes, vendors – blending into a cacophonic mess. I stretched and ran a 2k, then had some coconut water, called home, and sat down to meditate. No plans, just sitting and I realised how much I missed it. I took out my notebook and made some quick sketches. I don’t remember the last time I had time to sketch. Sorry if this is getting grim, I also thought what the hell was I doing.

Funnily, I looked around sitting at my shade of coconut trees and found people hunched over their phones. I wondered how I have spent thousands just for a few hours of not looking at screens. What world have we created? People don’t value what they have and keep running for things they don’t need. I was reminded of the following verse from the Quran: “Surely, humanity is in grave loss” (103:2).

I had some millet dosa at a local tiffin shop and went out for a solo sight seeing. I went to all the museums, the inside of a submarine and other aircrafts. Vizag is a naval base, apparently so you can also spot multiple frigates on the sea horizon. I was annoyed by a lack of fibre/protein food options, just had some egg bhurji and plain roti at a local shop and my stomach groaned in disagreement. I passed by an officer’s mess and I envied their lives a bit - sure maybe for their exclusivity but also for their discipline. I envy their discipline and structure in life.

I trekked up to Kailasgiri hill and thought it would be quiet but forgot to factor in the fact that it was Sunday. I was surrounded by so many people and yet I was all alone with no one to disturb me. I spent some time relaxing and some time meditating. The trek back was much easier, they have proper stairs cut out.

My friend had given me some food places to try so I booked a Rapido from the Zostel. I have never paid 34 rupees for 3km for a bike ride. It felt strange. The blast of freezing air from the AC and the context switch from the sweltering 43 degree heat made me turn from sweating like a pig to a frozen popsicle in minutes. Vizag people are built different. The place was called Subayya Gari hotel. I looked around, it was white, sterile with warm overhead lights. There were a few families quietly eating at various corners. There was no menu, no spoons on the table. Because there was just one item on the menu. Everything.

The person spread a large banana leaf in front of me and started putting items and rattling off in Telugu about the food with utmost dedicated. I just obediently nodded like a good boy and waited for him to finish serving. I thought it was basic manners. I had one of the most sumptuous meals that night - I forgot everything about my diet and asked for a second serving of all the rices. I decided to walk the 2km back to the Zostel.

I went to bed around 9:30pm. Enough adventure I thought to myself, it would be Monday the next day.

Day 3, 4, and 5 - A Cog in the Machine

Well, I just hanged around the resort at Sai Priya. I went out for morning runs along the beach in the sand and went for swimming at the pool at 5pm. I would get meals at the hotel inside the resort and work the rest of the day from my room. The saddest part was that the hotel folks didn’t bother to make a single person serving size, all their portion sizes were for two people so I always had to ask them to pack food which I would have the next day in the morning. Do these people think that a person cannot enjoy himself alone?

My friend was supposed to come back on Day 6 and we would take a train to the Araku valley, hold for a night and then go to his place for another night. However, his family didn’t allow so I had to cut short my trip by two days. I checked out of the hotel, attended some important meetings from the hotel lobby. I also saw a couple sitting hunched in front of their laptops just like me and I smiled. Blessed are those who have company. It’s the highest blessing.

I took my luggage, booked a cab and headed to the airport. My flight was at 11:40 at night, I had the whole day. I had to submit my thesis so I worked at it the whole day at the airport then bought an overpriced coffee from the food stalls. Once again, the solitude of the airport was allowing me to concentrate and I fired up my word processor to complete that blogpost I had on my mind for a long time. I secretly hoped to be seated next to a cute girl on the way back to perhaps lighten the mood or to have a chat with. The flight was 50% empty and both the other seats were empty as well.

“Well, that’s that”, I thought and stretched my legs like a sleepy cat. I tried concentrating on Amartya Sen but just stayed out of the window at nothing, letting my mind wander into a slumber only to be jolted really hard by turbulence. I couldn’t sleep after that and my mind was on alert. There was a lot of turbulence on that flight (apparently it rained in Delhi and it was very cloudy). I tried looking out the window but all I saw was the red flashlights on the wings diffusing into the clouds. I saw vast tracts of light dots zooming on the roads forming a complex network of veins and arteries. The city was alive.

I landed around 1am, took a cab and by 2am I found myself standing in front of my hostel room, all items right where I left them.

Thanks for reading this far, you are still here! Let me know of places I should go next!

Footnotes

  1. She has left the campus now, though.
  2. I am writing this from an apartment, and I have all “amentities” but I hate it. I honestly just hate it, all this comfort is making my bones weak and my soul hollow. I want to live like how our ancestors used to live. Not have the supply chain of industry and intricate capitalistic mechanisms provide all food, clothing, tools I could possible imagine served right on my table. I want the freedom, Idk of wandering around? Riding horses? Fishing?

item.title: Indians Are Really Bad At Picking Opponents
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
Disclaimer: This post is inspired by some recent incidents. Ashamed to be writing this but has to be written nevertheless. What follows might sound like blabber and ranting at points because that’s what it is somewhat. Then I figured I have stopped myself from writing just to, you know, wait for the day I “structure my thoughts properly”. And then realised, to my bitter dismay, that no such day comes. So here I am, putting some thoughts on paper, coherent or not you be the judge of that.

Introduction

India, as of 2026, seems to be suffering from a lot of problems. I don’t know if this was the usual amount of problems that we have faced as a nation – a devalued currency, social unrest, a radical nationalist destabilising force threatening societal peace, global insults, violence, societal evils, corruption, broken food system, broken education system – it almost feels like the more I grow, the more I acutely become aware of these issues and as a whole, I am sure perceptive people have felt it weighing down on them for what is our fault? We just want a respectable life.

The premise

Anyways, we suffer from issues. Then, we should try to solve them. But how do we even start thinking about them, classifying them, prioritising them? What is the most effective lever to tune for the maximum effect? I have been struggling with this question for quite some time and this is one way I think about it. The core premise is (as the eponymously named title): “Indians are really bad at picking opponents”. We don’t know who to pick fights with and what values to struggle for. Let me explain now.

Our opponents are uncles who have tried to overtake us at the airplane boarding line (who also in their head think of us as their opponent). Our opponents are farmers at sabzi mandis where we fight to bargain 10 rupees off the poor soul’s back, declare victory if we do or leave if we don’t. Our opponents are faceless bots in purposefully instigated hate posts on Instagram. As Indians, we are the most gullible of all humanity.

Who should be our opponents?

I remember last year (and in fact, every year’s distribe) of how Delhites go bonkers over polluted air during Sep-Oct. Rallies, protests, abuses hurled at whoever the CM is, and then Dec comes, down goes the AQI levels and everybody literally forgets that air pollution is still an issue. Ironically, the best time to combat air pollution is when there is no air pollution. This is exactly what Beijing did when their President literally “declared war on polluted air” and aligned people’s expectations and duties to nothing sort of a war. That is the kind of sustained mobilization that we lack as Indians. We are opportunists and egoist who love to blame and lament and sigh when things go wrong but are embarrasingly wrong at picking what to fight.

Our opponents should be the outflux of basic necessities like a reliable foundational AI stack, food security and rising energy and real estate cost. Our opponents should be fighting for clean food and clean water and clean air – the literaly bare minimums of a dignified life. I can only attribute to a lack of imagination.

Our “Rich” Cultural Heritage

The saddest part is that India is a rich enough country to provide for all but it is greed that has corrupted people’s soul. Our opponents are not vices but our own countrymen. I have observed it more often than not. For example, the coffee serving person refused to serve coffee to my colleague at the India AI summit saying its for white-skinned folks. This is literally free, open to all coffee. Another incident at a five star hotel where we faced racism. Yes, racism in 2026. In. My. Own. Fucking. Country. (where I pay taxes). Unfortunately, the post-colonial mindset is intact and thriving. People who say otherwise are delusional.

The last generation of Indians have never been affleunt economically and it shows in their psychological trait. The most interesting is the case study of the idea of “free”. Slap the “free” label on anything and watch Indians hoard over it like hungry zombies. There is something so hypnotically alluring about free things that Indians love. I recently came across this news where people were caught smuggling food from airport lounge. Yes, you read that right. Day after day, Indians export their manners to foreign countries and keep getting insulted and abhorred. For example, news of people stealing food from supermarkets in first world countries abound. I myself had a similar experience at Paris and I honestly just sadly conceded with my fate because that is the kind of impression those people chose to leave for their posterity. For us. To suffer and be humiliated. There are Indian students who make tutorials teaching other Indians how to get free food from food banks in foreign countries which are benevolent charities for homeless people. People are scamming welfare programs in India and abroad. What does all of it tell us?

I still come back to the idea that as Indians we lack imagination. Welfare programs are for folks who really cannot afford those basic necessities that we enjoy. As humans, as decent humans, we are the best judge of whether we truly need those welfare support or not. For 99% of us, we do not and yet we apply. We lack discipline, we lack empathy, and most importantly, we lack basic humanity, man. News of government run programs being gamed and thousands of crores of rupees being siphoned off, for example, recently the thousand crors fund setup for Startup India scam came into the light where the people who were the custodians of the fund were the one approving funds for their own startup. Day after day, Indians hit new bottoms. Indians continue to suffer from a lack of imagination.

The Deeper Problem

I think a deeper problems is a chronic inability to understand the idea of money and the concept of value. Our Indian minds are unable to comprehend the fact that value is unbounded, it is truly unlimited and it is human ingenuity and hardwork that creates value. We are not competing for the same slice of pie that we fear someone’s getting more pie means less for us. It is not a zero sum game. Ironically, value is created in a cooperative society, not an adversarial one. There is no limited buy. We can literally stretch and make the pie bigger. What stops us, again, is a lack of imagination.

This simple fact is lost from the top IAS officer scamming the latest PM whatever yojana - money to serve the poor, feed the poor, or educate the poor to pot bellied uncles sitting in the clerk level 1 of the govt bureaucracy whose job is to move files from one table to the next.

My hatred is not for the bureaucracy, it is the underlying metastructure that has precipitated the set of incentives that are in the absence of checks and balances. I was shaped by these early experiences with the bureaucracy since I was a child. I remember heading out to get a signature for some scholarship and I saw people in uniform, in broad daylight asking for bribe, just to move my file across the table. I was ten or eleven, I think.

The Dick Measuring Contest

Another peculiar thing I notice is what I call the dick measuring contest. A new disease that affects the educated and half-educated. The manner of conversation is as follows: Someone posts about X group facing Y disadvantage. Instead of trying to understand and solve the problem, these folks revert back with “Oh, didn’t group A also face B disadvantage?” Comparing apples to oranges, disrupting the flow of the conversation, effective stifling any chances of a meaningful way to reach a conclusion. It’s a way to nullify all attempts at arriving at the truth by diverting the flow of conversation to something inconsequential. To all these big heads all I want to say is it’s not a dick measuring contest.

Who Should Be Our Opponents?

Let me invert the question I asked earlier - Indians suffer from a lack of imagination. What happens if we let our imagination fly beyond our wildest dreams?

Wealth is the cornerstone of power in modern society (not really modern, of all society of all times). And yet as India, once the resource center of the world, 25% of Indians (roughly 350M in absolute numbers) live in poverty. These are folks who cannot afford basic healthcare, transport, education, food, and water. This blogpost is unreachable to them just as is unreachable almost 99% of the Internet and all of human knowledge, sealed in a language unknown to them, in an untoched ethereal medium. Think of mothers leaving their kid because she cannot feed her, think of kids with dreamy eyes as they try to sell toys at road crossing, think of that father who goes to bed hungry and battered by the sun. This is the country that some nationalists beat drums about, speak in superlatives of the greatness that was. This is my major qualm with this line of thinking. A nation that has lost its moral and philosophical vigour to arise and awake rests upon its laurel of its past and is complacent in the present. It is the spiritual duty of each nation to march forward or be forgotten as is evident in history.

Where did we lose it? I once read that one of the explanations for the lose of ambition and embracing of austerity has to do with our spiritual texts which are also really the foundational philosophical basis guiding the quality and way of life (Most likely it was Gurcharan Das’ India Unbound) Maybe, maybe not but seems like a good explanation to glue into my premise building narrative.

But also in those scriptures are mention of unparalleled abstract thinking - of invention of statecraft and politics (Think of Kautilya’s state policies and Shankarcharya’s magnificent debates), of invention of the concept of nothing, of astrology and astronomy and such a rich heritage of cultural philosophy (there’s a challenging philosophy to any.philosophy that you name) - what does it mean? What were these people trying to do? Prove each other wrong, boast of their “bigger” brain? No, something more profound. These people were curious and questions troubled them. It didn’t make them sleep. It made them wake up in the middle of the night and wonder. Wonder about the movement of stars and their own bodies. Questions of their very existence troubled them. Not how to fraud your brother of their rightful portion of the property. They had imagination.

Forget that, look closer home. Look at the string of global intellectuals we produce, people with strong world view altering thoughts and philosophies. We are not less than anyone - our likes compete with the likes of Kant and Nietzsche, heck, even Aristotle and Plato. We don’t shy away from complex ideas, we relish them. Once again, when did we lose that edge? When will we raise a Vivekananda again in every household? Not for seeking glory but for the simple pleasure of pondering existence. For picking better opponents.

Parting thoughts

Recently, I had a outburst kind of a moment on Instagram. It was related to news from past few months. Everyday news of how the food I am eating is actually. It’s almost like there’s a state of hopelessness amongst people. Like there’s no hope that an attempt to escape the matrix may be successful. Each time someone tries someelse puts them back into the rotting pot. And for a people, they maybe defeated but they must never be hopeless.

item.title: The society we are engineering and the death of manners
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
I think the greatest travesty of our time is that a boy is unable ask if a girl sitting on an adjacent middle cramped and crappy seat on an indigo flight for 2 hours with lots of sleep in her eyes, can rest her head on his shoulder and get a good sleep. Not for any romantic interest. Not for any “ulterior motives”. And definitely not to “get into her pants”. But just as one of the last remnants of human decency and basic manners. For why should any girl not be able to sleep comfortably on a flight?

And yet we have engineered a society which makes it increasingly difficult to affect such moments of courtesy and chivalry. A society which questions, nowadays, even if you offer a hankerchief to a pretty girl and examines your action with the most judgemental and scornful of eyes. Ironically, these folks have never been the affecter and neither the receiver of such courtesy in their own lives. What society are we building if a simple act of asking “Are you okay?” sends the humble human mind into countless internal conundrums and questions and contradictions – that human mind which has been conditioned for millions of years to help and provide for the community and find rejoice and purpose in it? Why should it be so hard to be kind? We must ask ourselves a million times? Why? Why? Why? Isn’t a kindness done to others somehow able to find it’s way back to us? Then how can we, no, why should we expect others to be kind to us in times of our direst needs?

item.title: Reflections on the Mahabharata
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
“A steady mystic stays the same / In infamy as well as fame” ~Bhagavad Gita

I have been trying to revive my reading habit and what better way than to read one of the greatest epics of all times?

I think the genius of the Mahabharata is not in telling a story but in enabling the reader to ponder on the thousands of what-ifs that could have branched out. This epic touches on almost all aspects of the human condition - there’s statecraft, religion, spirituality, politics, conduct, and character, all wrapped in the creative robes of mysticism and magic – talk of shape-shifters, demons (“rakshasas”), demi-gods, cool magical weapons (Sudarshan chakra and Arjuna’s Gandiva), Indra loaning out his weapons to Arjuna (and later, Karna) and just the unfettered mixing of the divine in the matters of the terrestrial.

In terms of literary plots, the Mahabharata is a masterclass in story-telling, there’s, of course, foreboding and the idea of the immutable character that just manifests before the act is carried out - for example, Shakuni’s malicious nature, the jealousy of Dhuryodhan, and the individual natures of each of the Pandavas.

I have read Amit Majmudar’s Mahabharata trilogy as I found it quite accessible and engaging.

The game of dice

The Mahabharata is a treat for statisticians and economists examining the very nature of causality (a problem plaguing humanity since time unknown). The most famous instance is the game of dice.

After losing everything, Yudhisthir remarks that the Gods have tested him and given him “everything back” when Dhritarashtra intervenes and orders that Dhuryodhan not be unreasonable and gives him everything back.

Was the game of dice really a test? And more importantly, did Yudhisthir really succeed by being patient or was he just stupid? The point is that Dhritarashtra’s decision to restore Yudhisthir’s wealth is not conditional on the outcome of the bet. Therefore, to associate his restoration as a consequence of his patience and piety is wrong, in my interpretation.

I think the deeper question is: for how long can the faithful afford to be faithful? The concept of the earthly world as an illusion and distraction and a test for the faithful as presented in the Islamic faith also urges believers to be patient (Quran 2:153) . However, for obvious reasons, being courteous, virtuous, and honest in an unfair, dishonest, and corrupt world leads to suboptimal outcomes for the practitioner of honesty; this is the classic prisoner’s dilemma problem in an uncoordinated setting where the Islamic system aspires to establish the coordination protocol. See Scott Alexander’s Meditations on Moloch .

Dharma and the Morality of Doing Right

I was about to write the morality of doing good in the heading but have understood that defining “good” is a much harder task than defining “right” which I define as doing maximal justice while affording kindness.

The Mahabharata reminds us constantly of the necessity of sticking to our values, of doing the right thing even though it may lead to suboptimal outcomes (loss, death, pain, misery) as you distort the trough of evil. What I like is how the lesson is subtle and hidden behind the predicaments of the characters, unlike, for example, the Quran where the lesson carries authority and a directive nature (Quran 2:155) .

Bhishma: “I will not abandon my war ethics even if everyone else around me has” said after he was informed of the abandonment of war practices by both the armies on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.
Some of the banger lines are, no doubt, due to Bhishma:

Bhishma: “I wish you victory but I will do everything to prevent it” said when one of the Pandavas came to seek his blessing just before the war.

The Mahabharata is replete with such conflicted dialogues (boons and curses and promises and vows) exposing the tension manifested in the decisions and stances that the characters had to justify. This is a much closer representation of how people form opinions and take sides in the real world.

The What Ifs

I can go on and on about the what ifs. There’s just so many things you can discuss at length, plots within plots, all forming an interconnected mesh of rich storytelling.

Once you read about the scale of destruction and loss and bloodshed in the Mahabharata, one question is most likely to arise: could it have been avoided? And then the mind follows each event in the causality chain and goes back and back? Would it have stopped if the Kauravas had not insulted Draupadi in the court of Dhritarashtra? Or, if Vyasa had not assisted in the birth of Duryodhan? Or what if Ambika had not closed her eyes on seeing Vyas? Or if Shantanu had not lusted over Satyavati? Or if Amba had not been wronged by that stupid prince? And on and on, we can go on until we arrive at the origin itself - the Creation. But there is no cause of the Creation, therefore, all events that follow it must be meaningless.

Good and Evil

The themes in Mahabharata are a reflection of the human condition. The plots and the subplots all recursively subscribe to the same or similar themes even if the plots are different, vividly imagined, and utterly creative. There’s the lust of men and men’s hunger for war. These are no-brainers. And then the idea of the opposites - the creation and the destruction. There’s the ideas of good and evil but these are very subjective. For example, the Mahabharata is traditionally narrated from the Pandava’s perspective so the reader is implicitly signalled to think of them as the “good” guys – exiled and unjustly wronged. Whereas the evil Duryodhan refused to follow customs, broke the rules of war and tradition and insulted the weak and dishonoured Draupadi. As a society, we associate Duryodhan’s character with evil, but why? Because they lead to societal instability. But from Duryodhan’s perspective, was he wrong? If someone ever wrote the Mahabharata from the Kauravas perspective, I think it will be hard to still justify the Pandavas as the “good” guys. Duryodhan was always second, the second-loved pupil of Dronacharya (Arjuna being the first), the second in strength to Bhima, second-in line to the throne after Yudhisthir, everywhere he went, he was bested by the Pandavas. And was it fair that Arjuna got his weapons as a gift from Indra? Or, that Krishna assisted the Pandavas on the battlefield? Is the divine a fair match for the earthly? And there is not less blood on the hands of the Pandavas either. And what about the dilly-dallying of Arjuna during his exile?

But this is in conflict with the central theme of the Mahabharata - the relativeness of good and evil. The non-absolute fluidity of labelling actions and events and thoughts and consequences as good or bad. And the very act of writing things down itself – the manner of writing is political.

Death, the Ultimate

Interestingly, the God of Dharma or justice is the God of Death, Yama. I think it’s a beautiful association. Death gives us urgency, a sense of belonging, and a purpose. It is the fear of death that motivates men. To create or to destroy. There would be no action if everyone was immortal. Everyone would just be bored.

(Ir)Responsible Men

There have been many kings and leaders and they have all been wise and being wise means choosing peace even when war is possible - especially when war is possible. Dhritarashtra could have prevented war but he just stood by like a bystander and blamed “dharma” or fate or whatever it is for what he knew was coming. I remember this quote by Dante Aligheri or someone

“The deepest place in hell is reserved for those who remain neutral in times of moral crisis” ~

This guy could have prevented war but he just stood by. In my opinion even to struggle against destiny is obligatory on man if it means peace. Especially when you know that your struggles and revolution would be met with no fruit. Peace and prosperity is the ultimate goal.

He reminds me of countless babus and people in authority today who have the power and position to bring about change but all they care about is wrongfully filling their own coffers while millions suffer - millions of humans who are starved, who do not have basic dignities of life - healthcare, home, clothes even, and education or a chance to better your condition. Every atom of my body and every strand of my soul hates such word weaving, action less men.

Conclusion

A lot can be said and discussed about the Mahabharata and a lot of more able people have done it before me already. These were just some of my scattered thoughts and reflections of what I found most interesting. Finally, I would like to end with some of my favourite quotes:

Do you fear disgrace, warrior? I thought you feared nothing, said Krishna to Arjun after being insulted by the Trigartas.

Paraphrased from the Gita:

Thy right is to work only, but never to its fruits; let not the fruit of action be thy motive, nor let thy attachment be to inaction.
All errors my own, please write to me if I made a mistake. Also, do write to me if you have a different take, I am up for understanding things better.

item.title: On Swimming
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
This post is not enlightening or profound or at least doesn’t pretend to me like my other posts. I am, honestly, just trying to find excuses to write more. There are just so many thoughts in my head these days. Not sure if all are interesting but some surely are.

In any case, I wanna talk about this new hobby that I have found. In truth, swimming is less of a hobby and more of an absolute necessity in this absurdly hellish summer in Delhi. So yeah, I have joined the IIT Delhi pool and been going three times a week for the past 2-3 weeks now. This is a stark decrease of 50% from last year and the year before when I used to go every single day (What can I say man, the joints don’t feel the same way?)

Anyone who has sunk their head underwater and released their breath in a slow controlled manner will testify to the utter peace and calm you feel. No wonder underwater meditation is a thing and even Dhuryodhan did it at the end of Mahabharata! It just feels so natural to be inside water, you know - feels like my domain in some sense1. Why?

A safe space

It’s because when I am underwater, the noise completely shuts down. The chaos and the oppressive meaninglessness of the daily drudgery wears off and for a moment, I feel free. Inside water, suspended by the chlorinated blue, I feel like I’m in my safe space. And even, physically, I mean. With no ground and the viscous fluid cushioning me, I feel like in the void, in total control of my motion, I can do a backflip or a frontflip or do anything I want. Control. Control. Freedom.

My restless mind

Swimming is not the first thing I have tried, of course. You see, my mind gets bored so easily and just completely shuts things off. It’s not just the privilege of being curious that’s enough but the timing and the location and a whole load of other factors needs to fall in place in order for a thing that you plan to be realised. I picked up Taekwondo again only to fail due to the disproportionate time that it was taking. Similar, I left studying Mandarin because there was no clear defined goal I was building towards.

What can I say? Being curious or hungry is not always enough. A ton of other things need to align.

The Domino Effect

I think it is no big surprise but by just focusing on one activity I have slowly been pulling up on other aspects like better nutrition, better sleep schedule. It’s like this domino effect when everything is in its right place . Optimising time for work and play and trying to learn to value my own time. I am currently thinking of starting running on alternate days to keep the cardio rhythm. But again, as any sportsperson will tell you, it’s not the initiation that’s hard - it’s the discipline to sustain.

Anyways, the other day I surprised myself by swimming 50 m. Now, I wanna crack 100 m. Upwards and onwards.

Footnotes

1: At least to me, it does. May not be a widely held belief.

item.title: Bonjour Monsieur: Paris '2026
item.author: gs454236@gmail.com (Basil Labib)
item.description:
I feel that my lack of attention to this blog cannot be compensated by me trying to apologise for it. But what can I say, man? Life happens. And I must say, I have been busy.

In this blogpost, I wish to record my experiences of my first European trip to Paris, the birthplace of art , style, and human finesse - not to mention, of revolution , liberty, and a number of incredible breads and other delicacies.

The prelude

This trip was a company retreat and thus was very kindly all-paid. Deliberations began in December of last year when I was first told of the retreat. As everyone was busy with the India AI Impact Summit, visa and other related processes continued to get delayed, eventually we booked the flights via Air France (one of the worst flight experiences I have had but more on this later), I submitted my visa application on the French visa website and booked a slot for my visa appointment via VFS website for Thursday (Jan 29th).

The one-day trip to Mumbai

The premium lounge service was a life-saver as I went to the Mumbai VFS office for appointment - yes, a one day trip to Mumbai from Delhi and missed one of my course tests.1 I set out very early around 4am and reached Mumbai’s Bandra-Kurla Complex around 9am. As I had lounge service, I was ushered in ahead of my appointment time and they printed all my docs without any extra charge. The process was a breeze except for a minor hiccup where I had filled my application with Delhi as my place of submission. I just refilled a new application and we were all set. My flight back was around 8pm so I went to Juhu beach, basked in the lovely sun (Delhi people don’t see the sun in the month of January), and soaked my feet in lukewarm oceanwater. I felt healed. I grabbed some delicious noodles at China Gate and set out for the airport. The best part? The visa was processed the next day and I received it on the morning of Saturday. It was crazy.

The preparation

The rest of February went in a flash with a fine balancing act of work and study. The India AI summit was from 16th to 20th, the retreat was from 24th Feb to Mar 1st, and my mid-term exams were sandwiched between these two on 21st and 22nd. Phew.

I studied as much as I could, bombed one exam and did fairly decent in another. My supervisor had very kindly agreed to allow me to send in a recording for my mid-term masters project on the condition that I submit a week before the presentation date (27th Feb)…which I never did. I submitted on Feb 27th while in Paris at 1am CET but we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

The summit had left me drained as I had anticipated with more than 350K people and 500 events - it’s kinda hard not to be overwhelmed by Indian things - all scale and grand - the big fat Indian AI summit. Results? Well, that’s the topic for another post. All I was looking for was a place to wind down a bit.

Day 1 - The arrival (24th)

Our Air France flights were scheduled for 1:30 am on the 24th so I reached the IGI T3 airport around 6pm on 23rd. I got off the wrong foot with VA over some shortcomings on my part but I just tried to avoid any unnecessary scuffle. Do also note that I was fasting since Ramadan had started and I was on average in a sour mood so to speak. We were supposed to be four people on the flight - VA (who flew from his hometown to Delhi that evening), JJ (who also flew from his hometown that evening), SSY (who was supposed to fly from Hyd), and me. SSY’s flight from Hyd to Del got delayed due to weather and he had to miss the Air France flight. He had to book a different Air India flight and he arrived in Paris 12 hours late (SSY’s trip was unfortunately marred with bad lucks).

In any case, we cleared immigration, security, and onboarded the flight. SSY’s seat was auctioned by the airline to a French lady for 5000 EUR or similar. I was in the middle seat with another Indian guy to the window. The French girl in the safety video commericial was kinda cute. The flight was for nine hours and a bit of a pain - the food was okay-ish, the seats not very comfortable, but it was night and I tried to sleep for most part of the trip. I scrolled their entertainment system and sadly didn’t find much options. I just put on some Charles Aznavour music and dozed off to sleep to the melody of this French guy rolling a lot of his vowels. The occasional announcements in French were going over my head but my inner linguist was jumping with joy because he had fodder for the next week to assimilate. I started mapping French to English and no surprises, it was semantically almost identical. I wager that if I spend 6 months in France, I would be able to understand and speak French. I started watching Lanthimos’ new movie Bugonia during the last hour or so of the flight.

We landed on time around 6:30 am CET, took a Uber (for 90 EUR!) to our BnB in the Auteuil area on Rue de la Fontaine (Rue means street). I picked up a free French airline magazine along the way. That was around 30km and a 90 mins ride. We checked into the BnB and SS (one of the other members from London) was already there and he headed to IASEAI conference. Me and the India delegation relaxed a bit and went straight to a Carrefour hypermarket. These are basically places to find literally everything like Tesco in London. There were other options too like Monop, Monoprix, and other local vendors. It felt like you could just roam around and buy the whole world haha! We got a lot of packaged food, yoghurt, vegan milk, spreads, breads, and necessary groceries. The bill was a modest 150 EUR and we carried everything back to base camp. A walk of 15 mins with the Parisian sun ushering in hope and casting away the sad drudgery of Delhi. The obvious thing to note were the architecture, of course. Just looking at the harmony of these buildings gave one a kind of inner peace. Truly, Parisian knew what value art holds in the daily mundane. I made a mental note of looking up Haussman who was appointed by the king to make Paris look pretty.

Rest of day 1 went in having some food, relaxing, going for a walk around the neighbourhood (I could use my cellular data for maps thanks to my Airtel international plan), and doing some basic work.

One qualm that I often have with Europe is, of course, the lack of a water spray in the washrooms. This basically meant that I had to wipe my ass and pretent everything was okay for the next six days. Abominable!

Even roadside cafe menus were undecipherable on day 1 so google translate was a big help. By day 5, I was able to make sense of things written. It almost felt like primitive code breaking.

The first walk

The sun rose late around 7:45 am and set later than the tropics. Combined with my jet lag, I felt a bit disoriented. I called folks back at home and they were 4.5 hours ahead of me - I showed them the view outside my room. While on my evening walk, I passed through a church, a hospital, and went to Parc Sainte-Perine, I saw Parisian grannies and grandpas relaxing on park benches, reading books while basking in the temperate sun. Paris realises the image of the stories we were told as kids - the post independence education that I was given that still reeked of the colonial undertones and inadvertently borrowed elements from our colonial overload’s culture. In India, such realisation of dreams is an impossibility due to the sheer numbers and the hawkish distribution of wealth and resources. I quietly observed kids playing in the park, their milky white skin, and golden brown hair being tousled by the Parisian breeze as they played football. Not a single building facade had a blemish - how can you expect such people who take such delicate care of their buildings to not take care of themselves? The soft cold breeze kissing my face competed with the sun’s sweet rays sometimes.

On Why We Take Pictures (and explaining the sales of cameras)

While we were on a bridge over the Seine (Port Mirabeau), I was trying to make sense of why people take pictures. Almost every human action can be traced to human insecurity just like in this case as well. At the bridge, we were not sure of what we were supposed to do and so in order to save our faces from embarrasment, we took out our phone and started clicking pictures. The invention of the camera was to fill our meangingless lives with an activity - something we can point to and say, “Oh, this is what I was doing”. The phone enables our lazy minds to feel accomplished - that’s all.

VA was coordinating with SSY throughout who reached quite late at night. Leaving the comforts of Swiggy and Zomato back home, here I scrolled through Uber Eats and tried to make sense of the menu items via translate.

VA, JJ, and me went for another walk to a shopping mall (Beaugrenelle ) on the other bank of the Seine to buy jackets for me and VA as mine was too worn out. I scrolled through Uniqlo, Nike, Levi’s, H&M, and others. The Northface one which I liked was 310 EUR so I calmly put it back. We just had some microwaved leftover from the afternoon meal and went to bed. There was Bolt and Lime for commute as well and funny sounding payment apps like Zuplee and Upplee. I remembered I had Bumble installed, I quickly installed Hinge and setup a profile. I swiped for a bit with absolutely zero expectations partly because I was in Paris only for 5 days. It was the usual French crowd - coiffeurs (hair stylist), etudiants (students), and bakers. It was definitely a notch above the average Delhi crowd.

I slept very early around 10:30 or 11pm.

Day 2 - The migration (25th)

I woke up at 5 am and it was pitch dark! The sunrise was in about 3 hours! I scrolled through Hinge and saw a reply from a girl from Brest. I liked how girls were more forthcoming than those in India who play pathetic mindgames. I really appreciate this quality as I don’t have to second guess what their intentions are. Although, the match didn’t go anywhere, it still felt nice. I tried to make the least amount of noise as I was aware that the walls are really thin in the West.

I went for a long walk around 8am and covered more than 2kms. I just loved walking around. That’s when I saw the Eiffel tower from the west bank of the river along Boulevard Exelman. No matter what you do, I felt that this city amplified everything. It can bring out your inner philosopher, your inner arist, or your inner scientist. It can make a man’s heart resolute and curios again - something that cities should do. Maybe I am romanticising Paris too much but whatever. It’s worth it.

As I passed by half-opened bakeries (la boulangerie) selling all kinds of lovely breads - buttery croissants, pain au chocolat, pain aux raisins, the sweet smell of freshly baked bread at these locally run Parisian bakery felt like a siren ushering you towards it. I was a bit late as VA had already woken up and called me twice to get back so I abandoned my plan to walk to Eiffel tower (that was a 30 mins walk according to Google maps). I got a bit lost at the cross-roads which still felt a bit confusing. I ended up at the same shopping mall as last night and hurried back to the BnB.

And then it started. The noises. Drilling and hammering and construction. It got so bad that we had to abandon the BnB and VA found another one on Rue de la Croulabarbe. We packed out stuff and just headed out in the Uber. I already had a heavy headache but the cab ride through the city made my headache kinda vanish. I saw lazy Parisians roaming the streets at 4pm(!), sipping coffee, smoking cigarettes in stylish clothes sitting on chairs outside cafe, drudgery in their eyes and no hope - the quintessential Parisian just as I have seen in Godard’s and Truffaut’s movies. The city that cures? Maybe.

An unpleasant experience

Although the cab ride cured, the cab driver was very unwelcoming - he was throwing our stuff around and talking haughtily - perhaps because of our colour. That’s when I got the first proper taste of the people of this city. Ironically, he wasn’t a native Parisian but an immigrant himself, I would hope natives would be more welcoming; I tried to justify his poor behaviour by trying to blame my fellow countrymen who might not have been on the best of their behaviour. But in any case, I felt horrible and my day was ruined. A similar slumber felt across the group. We just checked into the BnB which was more spacious and airy than the previous one. As a tiny shock to me, this BnB opened directly into the streets like there was literally just one quarter inch of steel between me and the wild west. I imagined it was a parking garage that the owner had repurposed into a residential suite. I shared my room with SSY. There was fancy wallpapers on the wall, pretty books on the shelves, and quirky painting hanging in the kitchen. I just hoped I could sleep in peace.

After wrapping up some work, me and the gang went out to find another Carrefour nearby (haha). We found one in Saint Marcel in the Gobelins area. VA bought some hot chocolate and a croissant from an artisanal boulangarie and the first bite of that inconspicous looking, cold piece of bread was enough to send me to a buttery delight - something about how these people make croissants, man. It was 100x better than what they dupe us back at home with. The neighbourhood felt way, way more like Europe - there were occassional Indian faces unlike London where every second face was non-Caucasian.

One thing I couldn’t help noticing was young people’s obsession with running. You can see them running literally everywhere. I really appreciate this - it has given me fresh impetus to take a deeper look at my own health. Health and taking care of oneself is not a very Indian thing. And in that gutter hole, you sort of forget what you are. And what you can do. You know, a sad environment kills curiosity and art and innovation. Sorry I got a bit cynical there.

We picked up some salads and bread from Carrefour and went to a McDonald’s. I had a McCrispy without bacon with fries and a very bad cherry flavoured coke which almost felt like medicine. That was our dinner. The walk back was 5 mins and I went to bed early as usual.

Day 3 - A sour experience (26th)

I woke up around 5 am and tried to complete some pending work and then dozed off again at 7am. I woke up again at 8am and saw the house was awake so I didn’t go back to sleep again. VA and JJ were supposed to head out to IASEAI conference yesterday but couldn’t due to the noise and unplanned BnB switching. They head out today leaving me, SSY, and SS at the BnB working.

Oh, did I tell you that there was construction work going outside the new BnB as well lol. They were building a new road just outside but the noise was much bearable and they finished before lunch. Day 3 was spent wholly inside the BnB in front of the laptop as I got reprimanded for wandering off for long the other day. SS went out for a “bit of movement” around 1pm, changed into running clothes and came back in an hour. He then changed and went away. And in India, there’s dumbnuts like Narayan Murthy screaming 70 hours work week lol. VA and SS came back earlier than expected, they didn’t get access to the venue and the receptionist was also being racist. It was unfortunate.

I had started making primitive relations between words and loved how the French fearlessly string their vowels like there’s no tomorrow. Auteuil for example.

Another unfortunate experience

The most unnerving experience for me, however, was the instance of blatant racism at Carrefour St Marcel. I was standing near the self check-out counters as SSY was getting the stuff billed when one of the coloured attendees exclaimed “Paaji, Chal, Chal” (literally, hey man, move, move!) in a tone that was more akin to herding sheep than a polite request to move. Honestly, I was too shocked to process what just perpetuated for a moment. I just looked at VA who gave me a knowing forlorn look - a look which expressed indifference and familiarity with such repeated abuses. I tried to justify the poor man’s behaviour by imagining the average Indian that he may have had to interact with and who might not have the eloquence of speech in a tongue familiar to him. And yet, somehow this empathethic garb could not veil the harm it had done. I was deeply moved by the experience and talked to my parents after it.

I had some of the packed croissants from Carrefour and even though, it was cold and packed - these were some of the most flaky, buttery goodness I have had. I can only imagine the heavenly taste of a freshly baked batch of croissants. SS ordered some vegan Japanese soup and fried sushis. Although the sushis were alright, the soup was beyond horrible. I just smiled and somehow endured through it. VA, however, is more outspoken and just blatantly expressed what he thought about the food.

Responsibilities from a past life

And inspite of these travesties of life, I was also conscious of my mid-term thesis presentation deadline and another assignment deadline. I quickly prototyped a system using Claude Code for my programming assignment and gave it a cursory read. I knew that the instructor was least bothered about the course so I also felt disinterested in putting in the effort given the tradeoffs. It was 10 pm already and I resolved to make the slides in the next two hours; God knows that making slides is the most agonising experience that man has ever had to endure. And yet I started, only for SS to propose that we play Exploding Kittens - a card game I had never played. My polite resistance felt to deaf ears as VA and others prodded me to participate. I conceded. It was a fun game and would become a daily post-dinner ritual at the retreat. I made some of my cherished memories during these games. It was, after all, a long time since I played such games - any game in fact.

When we were done, I looked at the clock and it was midnight. I groaned. I opened my laptop and opened Google slides only to find there was no Wifi! And then started another 40 minutes of debugging the Wifi and in the process completely dissipating the motivation I had collected for the final act. Great, I thought. In any case, I made some quick slides, recorded my video and submitted the presentation at some time past 1 am. I opened the door out of curiosity and found two figures embracing or sharing a smoke at a distance. The cold breeze froze my face. I shut the door and went to bed.

Day 4 - The meeting on a rainy day (27th)

I woke up around 8 am as expected and took a slow start. I called parents in the morning and listened to dad reciting Surah Baqarah and felt the most ease and warmth. I chronicled my incident from last night to my mother. In all the chaos, talking to parents is the best thing in the world - it felt like the only bit of grounding in an increasingly topsy-turvy world.

I made some fancy breakfast from all the groceries - toasted sourdough bread with hummus, guac, and choco spread, strawberries, some roasted nuts, and leftover sushis. I was getting fancy. I took a sip of the almond milk and was instantly reminded of the lice-killing concoction that my grandma used to apply to old wooden furniture. It was beyond horrible.
